newsitem.title: GERMANY: Opposition warns Kohl ahead of German tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Opposition warns Kohl ahead of German tax talks.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), on the eve of talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl over his plans for radical tax reform, warned on Sunday they were not prepared to accept key elements of his proposals.

SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said his party would oppose the government's scheme to abolish tax relief on working unsociable hours. Plans to cut the top rate of income tax and increase tax on pensions were also unacceptable.

"The SPD won't take part in any economic nonsense or break public trust. That means anyone who has to work on Sunday, on public holidays or at night won't face any additional taxes," Scharping told the daily Bild newspaper in comments to be published on Monday.

Government and opposition have been pushed into Monday's highly unusual top-level talks by Germany's biggest unemployment total since 1933 -- 4.7 million -- in a bid to stimulate investment and create new jobs as quickly as possible.

But the talks are not just about tax plans. They are also a high-stakes game of political poker as the government strains to meet the criteria for European monetary union and all parties try to position themselves for next year's general election.

Kohl appealed to the SPD to adopt a constructive stance, expressing optimism that the talks could send an important signal that Germany was ready to reform in order to maintain international competitiveness.

"Talks like these, between the coalition and the SPD, only make sense when everybody involved is ready to come to concrete results quickly. So there can't be any more party political showfights," he told the Welt am Sonntag weekly.
"Everyone will be thinking about their election chances," Scharping told the weekly Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung. "But eveyone should be thinking more about Germany's future."

The government needs SPD help to push through the reforms quickly because the opposition dominates the upper house of parliament. But while Scharping emphasised the SPD's willingness to negotiate, he doubted the talks could produce quick results.

"I would prefer if we could have a result after two or three rounds of talks," he said. "But I don't think that's going to happen. In fact, I'm very sceptical about whether the (government) coalition is capable of producing a result."

Some parts of the tax reform are controversial within Kohl's government, particularly plans to raise taxes on pensions. But the SPD is also far from united, especially when it comes to what should happen to the top rate of income tax.

Most SPD leaders reject Finance Minister Theo Waigel's concept of a cut to 39 percent from 53 percent but are divided on whether the rate should be cut at all, if so by how much, and if the income bracket for top earners should be revised.

But Scharping played down the importance of the issue. "All this talk about the top rate of tax gets on my nerves," he told Bild. "Before we talk about the top rate, we need to talk about the need to reduce the burden on normal earners."

No one is expecting a major breakthrough at Monday's first round of talks but agreement should be possible at some point in areas where the two sides are already close -- on a new bottom rate of income tax and on cutting corporate taxes.

The biggest barrier could be timing. Waigel wants most of the cuts to happen in 1999 but the SPD and even Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, are clamouring for bigger tax cuts a year earlier.
